title: Effect of the degree of wood use on the visual psychological response of wooden indoor spaces
research_question: What is the effect of different degrees of wood use (wood coverage and change of wood surface) on the visual psychological response (visual attention and psychological impression) of wooden indoor spaces?

participants.description: 75 university students (27 male, 48 female), aged 23-30 years, all with an architectural background; 30 participated in eye-tracking, interviews, and scoring; 45 only in scoring. 17 were familiar with modern wooden architecture.
participants.recruitment: Students were a readily available population for campus studies.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 12 computer-generated images of wooden indoor spaces, systematically varying in two physical attributes: wood coverage (6 levels: 5-20% to 80-95%) and change of wood surface (6 levels: 2 to 7, based on number of wood types and application positions). These were grouped into 'low', 'medium', and 'high' degrees of wood use.

findings.mechanism: This range represents the optimal 'medium' degree of wood use for positive psychological effects.
findings.quote: psychological impression of wooden spaces was at the best level when the wood coverage is in the range of 35–65% and the change of wood interface is 4 level or 5 level.

mechanisms: Wood is a natural product, and its yellow-orange tones contribute to perceptions of warmth.
Large wood coverage can create a sense of restraint and make a space appear narrow.
Changing the wood surface (type and application position) can weaken feelings of enclosure, leading to psychological relaxation and intimacy.
Wooden indoor spaces provide a restorative environment, alleviating attention fatigue in fast-paced urban life.
implementation_implications: Controlling the degree of wood use at a medium level can achieve higher preference in indoor spaces.
Controlling the degree of wood use at a low level can optimize indoor space quality while saving wood, which is important for countries with scarce wood resources.
Designers should consider the change of wood surface (types and application positions) in addition to wood coverage to enhance visual psychological responses.
These findings provide guidance for designing healthy and sustainable indoor environments that support human well-being.

limitations: The study used two-dimensional color images, which may limit the ability to judge preference without a broader environmental context.
Stimuli may constrain the environmental experience, particularly regarding the perception of sounds and light in real architectural space.
More research is needed for different design, structures, building functions (e.g., hospitals, schools, workplaces, nursing homes), and diverse populations (different ages, health conditions).
